newsitem.title: MAURITANIA: Mauritania parliamentary poll to test democracy.
newsitem.headline: Mauritania parliamentary poll to test democracy.

text.p: Mauritania, a bridge between Arab and black Africa, votes for a new national assembly on Friday, with opposition candidates and women seeking seats there for the first time.

Almost 1.1 million voters are eligible to take part in the latest test of the fledgling democracy which took root in the mainly Moslem West African nation with multi-party elections in 1992. Polls open at 7 a.m. and close at 7 p.m.

Supporters of President Maaouya Ould Sid'Ahmed Taya in the Democratic Social Party won 67 of the assembly's 79 seats in 1992. The ruling party, the only one contesting seats in all 53 constituencies, is confident of winning a fresh majority.

The opposition, which boycotted the 1992 poll denouncing irregularities, is hoping to make its mark ahead of a presidential election due by January 1998 in the impoverished, sprawling nation at the Atlantic fringe of the Sahara Desert.

The governor of Nouakchott, Mohamed Ould M'Reizim, who is responsible for polling in the capital, paid tribute to the calm that prevailed during campaigning and sharply rejected opposition predictions of fraud.
"The administration has taken measures to ensure that everyone has an equal chance," he told state radio on Thursday. "If there is fraud, sanctions will be applied strictly and scrupulously."

Opposition heavyweight, Ahmed Ould Daddah, runner-up to Taya in the disputed 1992 presidential election, accused the authorities of denying opposition parties a fair hearing in state media during the campaign, which ended on Wednesday.

"What we have experienced during the campaign, that is the systematic censorship of our speeches and our interventions, augurs ill for these elections," Ould Daddah, leader of the Union of Democratic Forces-New Era, told French radio.
He denounced corruption, falling purchasing power and rising unemployment.
But the main influence on the poll could be the attitude of the electorate -- many of whom failed to collect their voting cards by Sunday's deadline, which was extended to Wednesday.
Dominant light-skinned Moors of Arab stock and blacks each make up a third of the 2.2 million people in the arid, former French colony which won independence in 1960.
Arabic-speaking ex-slaves make up the remainder. The government formally banned slavery in 1980.
Taya, a French-trained army colonel, seized power in a bloodless coup in 1984. He launched a 1991 democratic transition and won a six-year term as president in 1992.
Thirteen political parties will contest Friday's poll along with 52 lists presented by independents -- mostly disgruntled members of the ruling party bounced off the party ticket.
Most of the 26 women candidates are from the ruling party.
First results are expected on Friday night but the final results could take a couple of days to emerge. A second round is planned for October 18, where candidates fail to secure an outright majority.
